ladder.what: A low-pass filter built like a transistor ladder (the same code as Kalliope's): it lets the low frequencies through and takes away the highs.
ladder.does: Below CUTOFF the sound passes; above it, it's turned down more and more the higher you go: -12 or -24 dB for every octave (SLOPE). RESONANCE feeds some of the output back in, which boosts a narrow band right at the cutoff. DRIVE pushes the sound into the filter harder for warmth and grit.
ladder.why: A raw oscillator is harsh and static. The filter is the main tone control of a synth: lower CUTOFF and a bright saw turns dark and warm; move it and the sound comes alive. Subtractive synthesis, the way most analog synths work, is exactly this: start bright, take away.
ladder.where: Between the oscillator (or a Mixer of oscillators, or noise) and the VCA. An envelope into CUTOFF makes each note open and close; MIDI In's PITCH into KEY keeps high notes as bright as low ones.
try: Play and sweep CUTOFF from top to bottom.
RESONANCE at 0.7, then sweep again: the classic 'wow'.
An envelope into CUTOFF with CV at 4 (lesson 4).

cutoff.what: The frequency where the filter starts cutting, from 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
cutoff.does: Everything above it is turned down; everything below passes. The knob is spread evenly by octaves, so each turn moves it by the same musical amount.
cutoff.why: It is the brightness of the sound: the single most played knob on a synth.
try: Play a low note and sweep it slowly: the sound goes from muffled to open.
Link it to a knob on your controller with LEARN.

res.what: Resonance: a boost of the frequencies right around the cutoff.
res.does: The filter feeds part of its output back to its input. A little makes a peak that sounds vocal and nasal; a lot makes it ring and whistle at the cutoff; near the top the filter oscillates by itself, a pure tone even with no input.
res.why: Resonance is what makes a filter sweep sound like a sweep: the peak travels with the cutoff. It's the squelch in acid bass parts and the 'wow' in a synth brass.
try: Turn it right up, unplug the IN: the filter whistles on its own. Plug MIDI In's PITCH into KEY and the whistle follows your notes.

cv_amount.what: How far the CUTOFF input moves the cutoff, in octaves for a full-size signal (0 to 8).
cv_amount.does: An envelope going 0 to 1 with this at 4 opens the filter 4 octaves above where the CUTOFF knob is, then back. An LFO going -1 to +1 swings it 4 octaves either way.
cv_amount.why: It sets how much a modulation does, without changing the modulation itself: the depth of the sweep.
try: With an envelope plugged into CUTOFF, set the CUTOFF knob low and turn this up from 0.

drive.what: How hard the sound is pushed into the filter (1 is clean, 8 is hot).
drive.does: The input is turned up before the filter, so its transistor stages saturate: rounded, thicker, then gritty. Lots of drive also tames the resonance.
drive.why: Warmth and dirt, inside the filter, where it sounds most natural.

slope.what: How steeply the filter cuts above the cutoff: -12 dB or -24 dB per octave.
slope.does: -24 (four stages) is steep: the highs vanish quickly, a round, fat sound. -12 (two stages) lets more through: brighter, buzzier, and the resonance sounds different.
slope.why: Two characters from one filter: -24 for deep basses and smooth pads, -12 for brassy, cutting sounds.

in.why: A filter shapes what it's given: plug in something with plenty of harmonics (a saw, a pulse, noise) for it to work on.
in.where: From an oscillator, a Mixer, or noise.

cutoff.what: Cutoff modulation: a signal that moves the cutoff, scaled by the CV knob.
cutoff.does: It's added to the CUTOFF knob in octaves, so the knob sets where the movement starts from and the signal moves it from there.
cutoff.why: This is how a filter moves by itself: the sweep on each note, a wah, a rhythmic pulse.
cutoff.where: From an envelope (a sweep each note), an LFO (wah), VELOCITY (harder is brighter), the mod wheel.

key.what: Keyboard tracking: a pitch signal that moves the cutoff along with the notes.
key.does: It moves the cutoff one octave for each octave of pitch, so the cutoff stays the same distance above every note.
key.why: Without it, a filter set nicely for low notes makes high notes dull (their harmonics are above the cutoff). With it, every note has the same brightness.
key.where: From MIDI In's PITCH, or a Sequencer's.

out.why: On to a VCA so notes start and stop, or a Mixer, an effect, or the Output.

ota_filter.what: A four-pole low-pass filter built from OTA chips (the same code as Kobalt's filter): rubbery and aggressive.
ota_filter.does: It works like the Ladder Filter (CUTOFF, RESONANCE, CV, KEY), but each of its four stages saturates on its own. Push a loud, resonant sound through it and it buzzes and squelches rather than getting louder.
ota_filter.why: Filters aren't all the same: the same settings sound different through each. This one is punchier and rougher than the smooth Ladder, good for basses and leads with bite.
ota_filter.where: Between the oscillator and the VCA, like any filter.
try: Build the same patch with the Ladder and with this, and switch the cable between them.
RESONANCE high, a short envelope into CUTOFF, a low saw: a rubbery bass (lesson 8 uses it).

svf.what: A state-variable filter: one filter with three outputs, low-pass, band-pass and high-pass, all at once.
svf.does: It works around one CUTOFF like the others (with RESONANCE, CV and KEY), but you choose what to keep by which output you plug in: below the cutoff (LOW), around it (BAND) or above it (HIGH).
svf.why: Not every sound wants the highs taken off: a high-pass thins a sound out (hats, airy pads), a band-pass leaves a narrow band (snares, voices, telephone). It's also the clearest way to learn what each filter type does.
svf.where: Like any filter, between a source and a VCA. Noise into it is the start of most drum sounds.
try: Play a saw through it and move the cable between LOW, BAND and HIGH.
BAND with RESONANCE up and an LFO into CUTOFF: a talking wah.

low.why: The usual synth filter: warm and dark as the cutoff goes down.

band.what: Band-pass: only a band of frequencies around the cutoff; the lows and the highs are both cut.
band.why: Thin, vocal, nasal sounds: snares from noise, telephone voices, wahs. With RESONANCE up the band is narrower.

high.what: High-pass: what's above the cutoff; the lows are cut.
high.why: To thin a sound out: hi-hats from noise, airy pads, taking the mud out of a busy patch.

envelope.what: A shape that plays once each time a note starts: up, down a little, held, then away when you let go. The four stages are Attack, Decay, Sustain and Release (ADSR).
envelope.does: When its GATE opens, ENV rises from 0 to 1 (ATTACK), falls to the SUSTAIN level (DECAY) and stays there while the gate is open. When the gate closes it falls to 0 (RELEASE). It doesn't make sound: it moves something else.
envelope.why: Real instruments don't switch on and off: a piano strikes and fades, a violin swells, a pluck snaps. An envelope gives a synth note that shape. On a VCA it shapes the volume; on a filter, the brightness.
envelope.where: GATE from MIDI In (or a sequencer); ENV into a VCA's CV for volume, or into a filter's CUTOFF for brightness. Use one envelope for each.
try: A long ATTACK for a swelling pad.
SUSTAIN 0, DECAY short: a pluck.
A long RELEASE: notes ring on after you let go.

attack.what: How long the envelope takes to rise from 0 to full when the gate opens (1 ms to 10 s).
attack.why: Short attacks are percussive (plucks, basses, drums); long ones fade in (pads, strings, swells). A couple of milliseconds removes clicks without softening the start.
try: Turn it up to a second on a VCA's envelope and play chords: a string swell.

decay.what: How long it takes to fall from full to the SUSTAIN level (1 ms to 10 s).
decay.why: The 'shape' after the hit: a short decay to a low sustain is a pluck or a bass blip; on a filter envelope it's how fast the brightness goes.

sustain.what: The level the envelope holds at while the gate stays open, 0 to 1. It's a level, not a time.
sustain.does: After the decay it waits here until you let go. At 0 the sound dies away even while you hold the key; at 1 the decay does nothing.
sustain.why: Organs and pads sustain; plucks, pianos and drums don't. This knob chooses which.

release.what: How long the envelope takes to fall to 0 after the gate closes (1 ms to 10 s).
release.why: Short: notes stop when you let go (tight basses). Long: notes ring on and overlap (pads, bells). Too short can click.

gate.what: What starts and ends the envelope: opening it starts the attack, closing it starts the release.
gate.why: The envelope needs to know when each note starts and stops. Unplugged, it never runs.
gate.where: From MIDI In's GATE (your playing), or a Sequencer's or Clock's gate.

retrig.what: Retrigger: a trigger here starts the attack again, while the gate is still held.
retrig.why: Rhythmic pulses on a held note: a clock or an LFO's square here makes a held chord stutter in time.
retrig.where: From a Clock's 1/8 or 1/16, or an LFO's square.

env.why: This is the shape you plug into whatever should follow it.
env.where: Into a VCA's CV (volume), a filter's CUTOFF (brightness), an oscillator's FM (pitch drops).

inverted.what: The envelope upside down: 1 minus ENV, so it falls when ENV rises.
inverted.why: For things that should go the other way on each note: a filter that closes then opens, a sound that ducks as another comes in.

lfo.what: A low-frequency oscillator: an oscillator too slow to hear (0.02 to 50 times a second), used to move other things.
lfo.does: It makes a repeating wave, triangle, sine, saws, square or random, which you plug into a knob's input to move that knob up and down for you. OUT swings -1 to +1; 0..1 swings from 0 to 1.
lfo.why: Repeating movement: vibrato (pitch), wah (filter), tremolo (volume), swirling pulse width, random burbles. It's the second main source of movement after envelopes.
lfo.where: OUT into the input you want to move: an oscillator's FM, a filter's CUTOFF, PWM. The amount knob next to that input sets how much.
try: OUT into an oscillator's FM, that oscillator's FM knob at 0.03, RATE 5 Hz: vibrato (lesson 5).
WAVE Random into a filter's CUTOFF: burbling computer sounds.

rate.what: How fast it moves: from once every 50 seconds to 50 times a second.
rate.why: Slow rates (0.1 to 1 Hz) make sweeps and drifts; around 5 Hz is vibrato; fast rates get rough and buzzy, moving towards audio.
try: Into a VCA for tremolo and turn RATE up from 1 Hz to 30 Hz: from a pulse to a growl.

wave.does: Triangle and Sine go smoothly up and down; Saw up ramps up and drops; Saw down drops and ramps; Square jumps between two values; Random jumps to a new random value each cycle; Smooth glides between random values.
wave.why: The shape is the character: a sine is a gentle vibrato, a square a trill, a saw a repeating swoop, Random the classic 'computer' sound.

rate_amount.what: How far the RATE input speeds the LFO up or slows it down, in octaves.
rate_amount.why: So the speed itself can move: an envelope making the vibrato speed up as a note holds, the mod wheel controlling speed.

rate.what: Rate modulation: a signal that speeds the LFO up or slows it down, scaled by RATE MOD.
rate.why: A wobble whose speed changes: from an envelope, the mod wheel, or another LFO.

reset.what: A trigger here restarts the LFO from the start of its cycle.
reset.why: Without it, each note catches the LFO wherever it happens to be. Reset on MIDI In's GATE and every note starts its wobble the same way. Reset on a Clock and it's in time with the music.
reset.where: From MIDI In's GATE, or a Clock's BAR or BEAT.

out.why: Moves things up and down around where their knob is: pitch either side of the note, cutoff either side of the knob.
out.where: Into an oscillator's FM (vibrato), a filter's CUTOFF (wah), PWM.

unipolar.why: For things that should only go one way from their knob: a VCA (a tremolo that dips but never goes negative).
unipolar.where: Into a VCA's CV for tremolo.

sample_hold.what: Sample & Hold: on each trigger it takes the value of its input at that instant and holds it until the next trigger.
sample_hold.does: Whatever comes in, smooth or noisy, comes out as a staircase of steps, one per trigger. With nothing plugged into IN, it samples its own noise: random steps.
sample_hold.why: Random but in time: the bubbling, stepped 'computer' sound into a filter, random notes into an oscillator, or a smooth LFO turned into steps.
sample_hold.where: TRIGGER from a Clock or an LFO's square; OUT into a filter's CUTOFF or an oscillator's FM.
try: Leave IN empty, a Clock's 1/16 into TRIGGER, OUT into a filter's CUTOFF with RESONANCE up.
Then put a Slew after it: the steps become glides.

in.what: What to sample. Empty, it samples its own noise.
in.why: Noise gives random steps; an LFO gives steps that follow its shape (a staircase up and down); any signal is frozen at each trigger.

trigger.what: Each rising edge takes a new sample.
trigger.why: It sets how often it changes. Unplugged, OUT never changes.
trigger.where: From a Clock (in time) or an LFO's square (free running).

out.what: The held value: the input as it was at the last trigger.
out.why: A stepped signal to move other things.
out.where: Into a filter's CUTOFF, an oscillator's FM (random melodies), or through a Slew.

slew.what: A smoother: when its input jumps, its output glides there instead, taking a time you set.
slew.does: RISE sets how long it takes to climb to a higher value, FALL to sink to a lower one. Signals that already move slowly pass through almost unchanged.
slew.why: Glide (portamento): notes that slide into each other instead of jumping. It also rounds off steps from a sequencer or Sample & Hold.
slew.where: Between MIDI In's (or a Sequencer's) PITCH and an oscillator's PITCH.
try: Put it in the pitch cable, set VOICES to 1, RISE and FALL to 0.1 s and play legato.
RISE short and FALL long: notes snap up and slide down.

rise.what: How long it takes to climb to a higher value (0.5 ms to 5 s).
rise.why: For pitch: how long a glide up takes. Different from FALL, so up and down can feel different.

fall.what: How long it takes to sink to a lower value (0.5 ms to 5 s).
fall.why: For pitch: how long a glide down takes. On an envelope or gate it softens the drop, like a release.

in.what: The signal to smooth: anything that jumps.
in.why: Whatever you want to glide instead of jump.
in.where: From MIDI In's PITCH, a Sequencer's PITCH, or a Sample & Hold.

out.what: The input with its jumps turned into glides.
out.why: The smoothed signal is what goes on to the oscillator (or wherever the jumpy one was going): that's where the glide is heard.
out.where: Into an oscillator's PITCH (glide), or wherever the jumpy signal was going.

vca.what: A voltage-controlled amplifier: a volume control that another signal turns.
vca.does: Its OUT is its IN times a gain from 0 (silent) to 1 (full). The gain is LEVEL plus the CV input scaled by the CV knob. With LEVEL at 0 it's closed until something opens it.
vca.why: An oscillator never stops on its own. The VCA is what lets the sound through when a note plays and shuts it when it ends; an envelope on its CV shapes that. It also does tremolo, velocity and any other change of level.
vca.where: After the oscillator or filter, before the Output. An envelope (or MIDI In's GATE) into CV.
try: Pull the cable out of CV: silence. Turn LEVEL up: the sound drones with no keys.
An LFO's 0..1 into CV: tremolo.

level.what: How open the VCA is before any CV: 0 is shut, 1 is fully open.
level.does: It's added to the CV input. At 0, only the CV opens it; turned up, the sound comes through all the time and the CV adds on top.
level.why: 0 for notes that start and stop. Higher for a drone, or to let a tremolo dip from full volume rather than from silence.

cv_amount.what: How far the CV input opens it.
cv_amount.why: Turn it down to make the envelope or LFO do less: a quieter note, a shallower tremolo.

response.what: How the gain follows the CV: Linear, or Exponential.
response.does: Linear: half the CV is half the volume. Exponential: the quiet end is much quieter, so fades sound smoother and more natural to the ear, and plucks snappier.
response.why: Our ears hear loudness in ratios, not steps: exponential fades sound even; linear ones seem to hang then drop.

in.what: The signal to turn up and down.
in.why: Usually the sound (an oscillator or filter), but it can be any signal: put an LFO through a VCA and the CV sets how much LFO gets through.
in.where: From an oscillator, a filter, a mixer.

cv.what: What opens the VCA: added to LEVEL, scaled by the CV knob, from 0 (shut) to 1 (open).
cv.why: This is where the note's shape comes in.
cv.where: From an envelope (notes), MIDI In's GATE (plain on/off), an LFO's 0..1 (tremolo), MIDI In's VELOCITY or MOD WHEEL.

out.what: IN times the gain: silent when closed.
out.why: The sound now starts and stops (or swells, or trembles) with the CV: this is what goes on to be heard.
out.where: Into the Output, an effect, or wherever the signal was going.

mixer.what: Adds up to four signals into one, each at its own level.
mixer.does: OUT is IN 1 times knob 1, plus IN 2 times knob 2, and so on. It doesn't care what the signals are: sounds or modulations.
mixer.why: Most inputs take one cable. The Mixer lets several things share one: two oscillators into one filter, an envelope and an LFO into one CUTOFF, noise added to a tone.
mixer.where: Before a filter (mixing oscillators), or before any input that needs more than one source.
try: Two oscillators, one an octave down, into 1 and 2: balance them with the knobs.
Add a little noise on 3 for breath.

level#.why: Balances input # against the others. Several loud inputs add up: turn them down if the result distorts.

in#.what: A signal to mix in, at level #.
in#.why: Any signal: a sound, an envelope, an LFO.

out.what: The four inputs, each at its level, added together.
out.why: One cable carrying everything mixed, for an input that only takes one.
out.where: Into a filter's IN, a VCA's IN, or any input that wants all of them.

attenuverter.what: Two signal adjusters, A and B: each scales a signal (smaller, off, or upside down) and shifts it up or down.
attenuverter.does: OUT A is IN A times SCALE A, plus OFFSET A. SCALE goes from -1 (upside down) through 0 (nothing) to +1 (unchanged). With nothing plugged in, OUT is just the OFFSET: a steady value.
attenuverter.why: Modulation rarely comes at the right size: this makes an LFO smaller, turns an envelope upside down so a filter closes instead of opening, or makes a fixed value to hold a pitch or a VCA open.
attenuverter.where: In the middle of a modulation cable: LFO → A → filter's CUTOFF.
try: Put it between an envelope and a filter's CUTOFF and turn SCALE A negative: notes start dark and open as they fade.
Unplugged, OFFSET A into an oscillator's PITCH: a fixed note to tune by.

scale_a.what: What IN A is multiplied by: -1 to +1.
scale_a.does: +1 passes it unchanged, 0.5 halves it, 0 removes it, negative turns it upside down.
scale_a.why: To set how much a modulation does, or flip its direction.

offset_a.what: A steady value, -2 to +2, added to A.
offset_a.why: Shifts a signal up or down: an LFO that swings 0 to 2 instead of -1 to 1. Unplugged, it's a fixed value of its own.

scale_b.what: What IN B is multiplied by: -1 to +1.
scale_b.why: The same as SCALE A, for the second channel.

offset_b.what: A steady value, -2 to +2, added to B.
offset_b.why: The same as OFFSET A, for the second channel.

a.why: Whatever needs to be made smaller, flipped or shifted.

out_a.what: IN A times SCALE A, plus OFFSET A.
out_a.why: The modulation at the size and direction you want, ready for the input it's meant to move.
out_a.where: Into whatever IN A was meant to move.

out_b.what: IN B times SCALE B, plus OFFSET B.
out_b.why: The second channel's result, ready for its input.
out_b.where: Into whatever IN B was meant to move.

ring_mod.what: A ring modulator: it multiplies two signals together.
ring_mod.does: Multiplying two tones gives their sum and difference frequencies instead of the originals: a 300 Hz and a 400 Hz make 100 Hz and 700 Hz. The result is rarely in tune with either, which is the point. MIX blends between A alone and the product.
ring_mod.why: Bells, robot voices, metallic and clangorous tones that a filter can't make. With an LFO on B instead, it's a deep tremolo that flips the wave's sign.
ring_mod.where: Two oscillators into A and B, then on to a VCA as usual.
try: Two oscillators into A and B, tune one with TUNE: hear the tone go from sweet to clanging.
A voice on A, an LFO at 8 Hz on B.

mix.what: How much of the ring modulation you hear: 0 is just A, 1 is all product.
mix.why: A little adds a metallic shimmer to A; all of it is the full effect.

a.what: The first signal: usually the voice being changed.
a.why: MIX at 0 passes just this, so it's the 'dry' sound.

b.what: The second signal, multiplied with A.
b.why: Another oscillator for bells and clangs; an LFO for tremolo.

out.what: A times B (blended with A by MIX).
out.why: The new, metallic tone: on to a VCA so it starts and stops with the notes.
out.where: Into a VCA, a filter, or the Output.
